lesson.title: Fertilization: Two Haploid Sets Become One Diploid Genome
lesson.summary: Fertilization is the fusion of a sperm and an egg into a single diploid cell, the zygote, restoring the full chromosome number and combining genetic material from two parents into one genetically unique individual.
lesson.body:
Fertilization is the fusion of two haploid gametes, typically a sperm cell and an egg cell in animals, into a single diploid cell called a zygote. This is exactly the event that gametes exist for. As covered in the previous chapter, meiosis produces gametes with only one set of chromosomes precisely so that fertilization can bring two haploid sets back together into a full diploid set, restoring the normal chromosome number for the species rather than doubling it further with each generation.

Fertilization is where the genetic contributions of two parents are finally combined into one genome. Because each gamete already carries a genetically unique combination of alleles, the result of independent assortment and crossing over during meiosis, and because fertilization typically involves essentially a random pairing of one gamete out of an enormous number produced by each parent, the resulting zygote ends up with a genotype that is, for practical purposes, unique. This makes fertilization the third major source of genetic variation in sexual reproduction, working alongside the independent assortment and recombination that already shaped the gametes themselves before they ever met.

In animals, fertilization generally begins when a sperm cell makes contact with and fuses with an egg cell, allowing the sperm's haploid nucleus to enter the egg and combine with the egg's haploid nucleus, producing the diploid nucleus of the zygote. In many animals, this fusion also triggers rapid changes at the surface of the egg that prevent additional sperm from fusing, a safeguard often called the block to polyspermy. This matters because it keeps the zygote's chromosome number correct. If more than one sperm nucleus combined with the egg nucleus, the resulting cell would carry more than two full chromosome sets rather than the normal diploid number.

The zygote formed at fertilization is the physical starting point for everything Mendel described through his breeding experiments, long before anyone knew what a chromosome was. Understanding exactly how that connection between chromosomes and inherited traits was made is the subject of the chromosomal theory of inheritance, taken up next.
